incidents.title: Minnesota State Patrol arrests CNN crew live on air in Minneapolis
incidents.summary: Minnesota State Patrol troopers arrested CNN correspondent Omar Jimenez and his crew on live television while they covered protests after the police killing of George Floyd. Officers gave no reason before handcuffing the three men; Governor Tim Walz apologized hours later and called the arrest a failure of the state's own procedures.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Protests in Minneapolis followed the police killing of George Floyd on May 25, 2020. Jimenez's crew was reporting live on the unrest and the state's response near the site of the killing when troopers moved to clear the area at dawn on May 29.
incidents.what_happened: Just after 5 a.m. on May 29, 2020, Minnesota State Patrol troopers in riot gear approached a CNN crew, correspondent Omar Jimenez, photojournalist Leonel Mendez and producer Bill Kirkos, reporting live from Minneapolis on protests over George Floyd's killing four days earlier. Jimenez identified himself on camera, showed his credentials and offered to move; troopers handcuffed him anyway, without giving a reason, and the arrest aired live. Mendez and Kirkos were also detained and the crew's equipment was seized. All three were released about ninety minutes later after CNN's president contacted state officials. Governor Tim Walz, Minnesota's head of government, apologized publicly the same day, saying the state bore responsibility for failing to protect journalists covering the unrest. CNN pointed out that a white CNN correspondent working nearby, Josh Campbell, was allowed to stay after identifying himself, a contrast that became part of the story.
incidents.stated_justification: Troopers gave no explanation to the crew before or during the arrest. State Patrol did not publish a contemporaneous justification; Governor Walz later called the episode a failure rather than defending it.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: CNN's live broadcast was interrupted by the arrest of an identified, credentialed crew, and the incident became one of the most widely seen examples in a wave the U.S. Press Freedom Tracker recorded of officers detaining or using force against journalists covering the 2020 protests nationwide.
incidents.status: Closed; the crew was released the same morning and Governor Walz apologized publicly.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: Minnesota State Patrol did not publish a named officer or a stated reason for singling out Jimenez's crew for arrest.
incidents.outcome_note: The crew was released within about ninety minutes and Governor Walz apologized the same day, calling the arrest his own failure.

claims.statement: CNN correspondent Josh Campbell, reporting nearby, was allowed to stay after identifying himself, while Jimenez was handcuffed.
claims.evidence_quote: I identified myself … they said, 'OK, you're permitted to be in the area.'

claims.value: Jimenez handcuffed on live television
claims.statement: Jimenez described the troopers who led him away as not violent, even as he was arrested without explanation.
claims.evidence_quote: As far as the people who were leading me away — there was no animosity there, they weren't violent with me.

claims.value: Walz apologizes, 2020-05-29
claims.statement: Governor Walz took personal responsibility for the arrest the same day.
claims.evidence_quote: This one is on me and I own it...I failed you last night in that.

claims.value: Contrast in treatment noted on air
claims.statement: A CNN anchor said the arrest reflected a broader loss of control by authorities managing the protests.
claims.evidence_quote: I do think what happened to Omar is part of a general loss of control.

incidents.title: Federal officers restrict press access to Portland protests; judge orders them to stop
incidents.summary: After federal officers deployed to Portland used tear gas, pepper spray and rubber bullets on journalists and legal observers covering protests, the American Civil Liberties Union sued, and a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction barring officers from dispersing, arresting or using force against clearly identified press.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The federal government sent Department of Homeland Security officers to Portland in July 2020 to protect a federal courthouse during nightly protests that followed George Floyd's killing; officers' use of force against bystanders, including identified journalists, prompted the lawsuit.
incidents.what_happened: Through June and July 2020, journalists and legal observers covering nightly protests in Portland, Oregon said police and later federal officers deployed by the Department of Homeland Security used tear gas, pepper spray, rubber bullets, flash-bang grenades and physical force against them even after they identified themselves as press, and in some cases arrested them or seized their equipment. The American Civil Liberties Union of Oregon sued on their behalf, seeking a court order to stop the practice. On July 16, 2020, U.S. District Judge Michael Simon issued a preliminary injunction barring officers from dispersing, arresting, threatening to arrest or using force against journalists and legal observers who could be identified by press passes, badges or distinctive clothing, and from ordering them to stop recording or seizing their equipment. The order, later extended and applied against federal officers as well, ran through the fall of 2020.
incidents.stated_justification: Federal and local officials generally described the use of force as necessary to disperse crowds and protect the courthouse and officers; no agency specifically justified using force against identified journalists.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Journalists reported being unable to safely document the protests and the federal response to them for weeks until the injunction took effect, after which the order gave them a specific, enforceable right to record police activity from a normal distance.
incidents.status: The preliminary injunction remained in effect through the fall 2020 protests, covering both Portland police and federal officers.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The full extent of federal officers' compliance with the injunction, and whether any officer was individually disciplined, was not established in the sources reviewed.
incidents.outcome_note: The court ordered officers to stop dispersing, arresting or using force against identified journalists and legal observers.

claims.statement: A federal judge granted a preliminary injunction protecting journalists and legal observers covering Portland protests.
claims.evidence_quote: This injunction is a critical protection for journalists and legal observers exercising their fundamental right to record and observe police activities at these important protests.

claims.statement: The ACLU said officers had used rubber bullets, tear gas, pepper spray and other force against journalists and observers before the injunction.
claims.evidence_quote: targeted journalists and observers with rubber bullets, tear gas, pepper spray, beatings, flash-bang grenades, detentions, arrests, and threats

claims.value: TRO sought June 30, 2020
claims.statement: The ACLU said the pattern of force had made people afraid to document the protests.
claims.evidence_quote: people are afraid to report on and observe protests because the police have targeted journalists and observers

claims.value: Order barred specific tactics
claims.statement: The requested order specifically listed the tactics officers were to stop using against press.
claims.evidence_quote: Using any form of physical force against a journalist or legal observer, including tear gas, pepper spray, rubber bullets, and flash-bang grenades

incidents.title: Political appointees alter CDC coronavirus guidance before public release
incidents.summary: Reporting in 2020 found that political appointees at the Department of Health and Human Services rewrote or edited the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's public coronavirus guidance and its weekly scientific bulletin before release, bypassing the agency's normal scientific review.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The reporting concerned the CDC's coronavirus testing guidance and its weekly Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report during the summer and fall of 2020, as the Trump administration sought to align public messaging with the president's own statements about the pandemic.
incidents.what_happened: Reporting published in September 2020 found that Michael Caputo, an HHS spokesperson, and an adviser he brought in, Paul Alexander, sought to change or delay CDC scientific communications, including the agency's weekly Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, so that public messaging would not conflict with statements President Trump had made about the pandemic. In one instance, HHS staff rewrote CDC coronavirus testing guidance and published it on the CDC's own website without the agency's normal scientific review, a document CDC officials later said did not reflect the views of many scientists inside the agency. Assistant Secretary Brendan Giroir said he coordinated input from task-force scientists but told reporters he did not know why some edits bypassed the standard review process. The episode became the subject of a congressional oversight investigation into political interference at the CDC during the pandemic.
incidents.stated_justification: Caputo told colleagues his goal was to "execute the president's agenda and to knock down any messaging, any communications that were seen as conflicting with what President Trump was saying about coronavirus."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Reporters covering the pandemic received CDC guidance and public statements that outside scientists said had been shaped by political appointees rather than by the agency's own scientific review, undercutting the reliability of official public health communications reporters relied on.
incidents.status: A congressional select subcommittee investigated the interference; no HHS official was reported to have been disciplined for the specific episode.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The full list of CDC documents altered by HHS political appointees, and which specific public statements resulted, was not fully detailed in the sources reviewed.
incidents.outcome_note: No agency reversal of the practice was documented in the sources reviewed; a congressional investigation examined the interference without a public admission of wrongdoing.

claims.statement: Caputo said his role was to prevent CDC communications from conflicting with the president's own statements about the pandemic.

incidents.title: Justice Department bars seizing reporters' phone and email records
incidents.summary: After it came to light that the Trump-era Justice Department had secretly obtained the phone and email records of reporters at The New York Times, The Washington Post and CNN, Attorney General Merrick Garland issued a policy barring prosecutors from using subpoenas or other compulsory process against journalists in leak investigations.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: In mid-2021, The New York Times, The Washington Post and CNN separately disclosed that the Justice Department had secretly seized their reporters' phone and email records years earlier while investigating leaks, including of information about contacts between Trump campaign associates and Russia.
incidents.what_happened: In 2021, the Justice Department notified The New York Times, The Washington Post and CNN that it had secretly obtained phone records, and in the Times' case attempted to obtain email records, from reporters during leak investigations that began under the first Trump administration, in one case accompanied by a nondisclosure order barring Times executives from disclosing the request. After the disclosures drew public criticism, President Biden called the practice "simply wrong," and on July 19, 2021, Attorney General Merrick Garland issued a memorandum barring the department from using subpoenas, warrants, court orders or civil investigative demands to compel journalists' records or testimony in leak investigations while they are gathering news, subject to narrow exceptions such as an imminent threat to life. A department spokesman said prosecutors would no longer seek such compulsory process against journalists doing their jobs.
incidents.stated_justification: The Justice Department said the new policy reflected that "a free and independent press is vital to the functioning of our democracy," and committed the department to protecting First Amendment values and journalists' independence.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The policy removed, for the time being, the threat that reporters covering national security and government leaks could have their phone or email records secretly seized by federal investigators, a practice that had already occurred at three major news organizations.
incidents.status: In effect from July 2021 until it was rescinded by Attorney General Pam Bondi in April 2025.
incidents.outcome_note: Attorney General Bondi rescinded these protections in April 2025, restoring the department's earlier discretionary balancing test.

claims.statement: Garland's memo barred the department from using compulsory process to obtain journalists' newsgathering records.
claims.evidence_quote: Because a free and independent press is vital to the functioning of our democracy, the Department of Justice has long employed procedural protections and a balancing test to restrict the use of compulsory process to obtain information from or records of members of the media.

claims.evidence_quote: will not seek compulsory legal process in leak investigations to obtain source information from members of the news media doing their jobs.

claims.statement: President Biden said the earlier seizure of reporters' records was wrong.
claims.evidence_quote: Absolutely, positively it's wrong. It's simply, simply wrong.

claims.value: Policy rescinded 2025-04-25
claims.statement: The department confirmed its commitment to press independence when announcing the policy.
claims.evidence_quote: The department strongly values a free press, protecting First Amendment values, and is committed to taking all appropriate steps to ensure the independence of journalists.

incidents.title: Police raid Marion County Record newsroom and publisher's home in Kansas
incidents.summary: Police in Marion, Kansas, led by Chief Gideon Cody, raided the Marion County Record's newsroom and publisher Eric Meyer's home, seizing computers, phones and files, on a warrant tied to an identity-theft investigation. The paper's 98-year-old co-owner, Joan Meyer, died the next day; a special prosecutor later found no evidence the paper had committed a crime.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Record had been investigating the driving record of local restaurant owner Kari Newell, who had accused the paper of accessing her personal information without authorization, the claim the search warrant cited as its basis.
incidents.what_happened: On August 11, 2023, Marion, Kansas police chief Gideon Cody led officers in searches of the Marion County Record's newsroom and the home of its publisher, Eric Meyer, seizing computers, servers, backup drives, cellphones and reporting files. The warrant cited an investigation into identity theft and unauthorized computer use tied to restaurant owner Kari Newell, whose driving record the paper had examined while verifying a tip. Eric Meyer's 98-year-old mother and Record co-owner, Joan Meyer, collapsed and died the day after the raid; the newspaper's staff attributed her death to the stress it caused. Local prosecutors withdrew the search warrants five days later, saying the evidence did not establish a sufficient link between the alleged crime and the newsroom. A special prosecutor's investigation released in August 2024 found no evidence Record reporters had committed a crime and said Cody would face a charge of obstructing the judicial process.
incidents.stated_justification: The warrant cited a criminal investigation into identity theft and unlawful use of a computer connected to how the Record had obtained information about Kari Newell's driving record.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The newspaper lost its computers, servers and reporting files for the length of the investigation, and the raid drew national attention to the use of search warrants against a working newsroom over a routine reporting inquiry.
incidents.status: The warrants were withdrawn in August 2023; former chief Gideon Cody faced a criminal charge following the August 2024 special-prosecutor findings.
incidents.outcome_note: Special prosecutors found no evidence Record reporters had committed a crime and moved to charge former police chief Gideon Cody.

incidents.title: Federal court strikes down Arizona's law banning recording police within 8 feet
incidents.summary: Arizona's 2022 law making it a crime to record police within eight feet after a warning was struck down by a federal judge in July 2023, who found it chilled a substantial amount of activity protected by the First Amendment and was not necessary given other laws already protecting officers.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The bill's sponsor said it responded to concerns that groups he described as antagonistic toward police followed officers around filming encounters and came dangerously close during potentially violent incidents.
incidents.what_happened: In 2022, Arizona Governor Doug Ducey signed House Bill 2319, making it a class 3 misdemeanor, punishable by up to thirty days in jail, to knowingly video record police activity from within eight feet after an officer warned the person to stop. News organizations and the American Civil Liberties Union sued, arguing the law would prevent journalists and bystanders from documenting police conduct, including alleged misconduct, from a normal filming distance. On July 21, 2023, U.S. District Judge John Tuchi permanently enjoined enforcement of the law, ruling it restricted a substantial amount of activity protected by the First Amendment without being necessary, since Arizona already had laws against physically interfering with police. Arizona's attorney general did not appeal, and the parties later entered a stipulated permanent injunction confirming the law could not be enforced.
incidents.stated_justification: The bill's Republican sponsor, State Representative John Kavanagh, said the law responded to groups he considered opposed to police that followed officers to film encounters and came dangerously close to potentially violent incidents.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Journalists and bystanders in Arizona had faced criminal liability for filming police from a normal reporting distance for more than a year before the law was enjoined.
incidents.status: Permanently enjoined; the law cannot be enforced in Arizona.
incidents.outcome_note: A federal judge permanently enjoined enforcement of the law, and Arizona's attorney general did not appeal.

claims.value: Bill responds to groups following police to film encounters
claims.statement: The bill's sponsor said the law addressed groups he considered antagonistic to police that filmed from dangerously close distances.
claims.evidence_quote: because there are groups hostile to the police that follow them around to videotape police incidents, and they get dangerously close to potentially violent encounters.

claims.evidence_quote: prohibits or chills a substantial amount of First Amendment protected activity and is unnecessary to prevent interference with police officers given other Arizona laws in effect.

claims.statement: The court found there is a clearly established right to record officers performing their duties in public.
claims.evidence_quote: there is a clearly established right to record law enforcement officers engaged in the exercise of their official duties in public places

claims.value: Statute did not survive strict scrutiny
claims.statement: The court found the statute was not narrowly tailored to a necessary purpose.
claims.evidence_quote: the statute does not survive strict scrutiny because it is not narrowly tailored or nece[ssary]

incidents.title: FCC chair reopens 'news distortion' complaints against CBS and NBC
incidents.summary: Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr reopened complaints alleging CBS and NBC distorted the news, demanding CBS turn over the full tape and transcript of a 60 Minutes interview and later accusing NBC's parent Comcast of misleading coverage of an immigration case.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The CBS complaint concerned 60 Minutes' October 2024 interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris; the NBC complaint, filed in April 2025, concerned coverage of the wrongful deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia.
incidents.what_happened: On January 29, 2025, newly installed FCC Chair Brendan Carr revived a 'news distortion' complaint against CBS over how 60 Minutes edited an October 2024 interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris, complaints his predecessor had earlier rejected as being at odds with the First Amendment. The FCC demanded CBS turn over the interview's full, unedited transcript and camera feeds; CBS complied on February 3 and 5, 2025, saying the broadcast was not doctored. On April 16, 2025, Carr said Comcast's NBC and MSNBC had spent days misleading the public about Abrego Garcia's case, and on April 21 the advocacy group Center for American Rights filed a complaint against NBC, ABC and CBS alleging misleading coverage, adding to investigations Carr had already reopened against the three networks in February.
incidents.stated_justification: Carr said Comcast's outlets had engaged in "news distortion" by, in his words, "implying that Abrego Garcia was merely a law abiding U.S. citizen."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: CBS turned over an unedited interview tape and transcript to a communications regulator under the threat of a broadcast-license investigation, while NBC, ABC and CBS all separately faced revived license-related complaints over their coverage of specific news events.
incidents.status: The complaints remained open, and Carr said he was open-minded about what action might follow.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: Whether the FCC would ultimately take formal action against any of the three networks' licenses was not resolved in the source reviewed.
incidents.outcome_note: The complaints against CBS and NBC remained open, with no formal licensing action announced in the source reviewed.

incidents.title: Congress cuts $1.1 billion in federal funding for public broadcasting
incidents.summary: At President Trump's request, Congress passed a rescissions package clawing back roughly $1.1 billion already appropriated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, eliminating federal funding for NPR, PBS and their member stations.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The rescission followed years of conservative criticism that NPR and PBS produced one-sided coverage, and came weeks after President Trump's May 2025 executive order directing agencies to stop funding the two networks.
incidents.what_happened: In July 2025, at the White House's request, Congress passed a rescissions package clawing back about $1.1 billion in funding Congress had already appropriated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting for the following two fiscal years. The House passed the package 216 to 213, with all but two Republicans in favor, after a Senate 'vote-a-rama' in which nearly every amendment failed along party lines; the measure became law on July 18, 2025. NPR chief executive Katherine Maher said public funding had supported a distinctive system of cultural and educational programming, while PBS chief executive Paula Kerger said the cuts would fall hardest on smaller and rural stations. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the package an affront to the normal appropriations process, while at least one Republican member said stations, rather than network editorial staff, would bear the consequences.
incidents.stated_justification: Supporters of the rescission cited long-standing conservative complaints that NPR and PBS produce one-sided news coverage that should not receive taxpayer funding.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: CPB's federal appropriation was eliminated, threatening the operating budgets of public radio and television stations, especially smaller rural and tribal stations that depend most heavily on CPB grants for local news coverage.
incidents.status: The rescission became law on July 18, 2025; CPB's federal funding was not restored.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The precise station-by-station effect of the cuts on local news coverage was not fully detailed in the source reviewed.
incidents.outcome_note: The rescission became law, eliminating CPB's federal appropriation; no restoration of the funding had occurred in the source reviewed.

claims.statement: NPR's chief executive said federal funding had supported a distinctive system of public programming that would now be lost.
claims.evidence_quote: Public funding has enabled the flourishing of a uniquely American system of unparalleled cultural, informational, and educational programming...

claims.statement: PBS's chief executive said the cuts would especially harm smaller and rural stations.
claims.evidence_quote: These cuts will significantly impact all of our stations, but will be especially devastating to smaller stations and those serving large rural areas.

claims.value: Rescission passed on party lines
claims.statement: Senate Minority Leader Schumer called the rescission package an affront to the normal appropriations process.
claims.evidence_quote: an affront to the bipartisan appropriations process.

claims.statement: One Republican member said anger at network editorial decisions should not fall on local stations.
claims.evidence_quote: If you're mad at the editorial people, that's fine. But you shouldn't be mad at the stations.

incidents.title: Trump sues Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over Epstein birthday letter story
incidents.summary: President Trump sued The Wall Street Journal, its owner Rupert Murdoch and two reporters for at least $10 billion, disputing the newspaper's report describing a bawdy letter he was said to have sent Jeffrey Epstein for a 2003 birthday album.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Journal had reported on a letter, bearing Trump's name and an outline of a naked woman, compiled into a birthday album for Jeffrey Epstein in 2003; the story renewed scrutiny of Trump's past relationship with Epstein.
incidents.what_happened: On July 17 and 18, 2025, The Wall Street Journal reported on a letter, featuring a drawing of a naked woman and signed "Donald," that it said had been compiled into a 2003 birthday album for the financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. incidents.title: Minneapolis police projectile permanently blinds photojournalist Linda Tirado
incidents.summary: Freelance photojournalist Linda Tirado was struck in the face by a less-lethal round fired by Minneapolis police while covering protests over George Floyd's killing, permanently blinding her in one eye; the city settled her lawsuit for $600,000 in 2022 while continuing to deny an officer had fired the shot.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Tirado was documenting the police response to protests over George Floyd's killing in Minneapolis when she was struck; a federal judge later found her case was one of numerous similar reports of journalists being hit by less-lethal munitions during the same unrest.
incidents.what_happened: On May 29, 2020, freelance photojournalist Linda Tirado was covering protests in Minneapolis over George Floyd's killing when she was struck by a tracking round and foam bullets fired by police; one projectile shattered her protective goggles and permanently blinded her in her left eye. Tirado sued the city, police officials and others on June 10, 2020. The Minneapolis Police Department did not respond to requests for comment on the incident. A federal judge, ruling on Tirado's case, found the allegations plausibly suggested a broader pattern, contrary to the First Amendment, of police intentionally using less-lethal munitions against identified journalists, since numerous other reporters described similar experiences during the same unrest. The city reached a $600,000 settlement with Tirado in May 2022, while continuing to deny wrongdoing and never acknowledging that an officer had fired the projectile that blinded her.
incidents.stated_justification: The city did not offer a public justification for the specific shot that struck Tirado and denied that any identified officer had fired it.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Tirado said the injury effectively ended a part of her career as a print photojournalist, though she continued working with adapted equipment; the case became a widely cited example of the physical risk journalists faced covering the 2020 protests.
incidents.status: Settled in May 2022 for $600,000; the city denied wrongdoing.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The identity of the officer who fired the projectile that struck Tirado was never confirmed by the city.
incidents.outcome_note: The city paid $600,000 in a 2022 settlement while continuing to deny that an identified officer fired the projectile.

incidents.title: FBI raids Project Veritas founder's home over Ashley Biden diary investigation
incidents.summary: FBI agents raided Project Veritas founder James O'Keefe's New York home and seized his phones as part of an investigation into the alleged theft of a diary belonging to Ashley Biden, President Biden's daughter, which the group had reported on; O'Keefe was never charged.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Project Veritas had obtained and reported on a diary purportedly belonging to Ashley Biden during the 2020 campaign; federal prosecutors were investigating how the diary had been obtained and transported across state lines.
incidents.what_happened: On November 6, 2021, FBI agents searched the Mamaroneck, New York home of Project Veritas founder James O'Keefe and seized two of his iPhones as part of a Justice Department investigation into the alleged theft of a diary belonging to Ashley Biden, daughter of President Biden, which O'Keefe's organization had reported on during the 2020 campaign. O'Keefe said the phones contained reporters' notes, confidential sources unrelated to the diary story and other newsroom material, and said it appeared prosecutors now had journalists "in their sights" for doing their jobs. His attorney said the underlying warrant cited potential charges including misprision of a felony and transporting stolen property across state lines. Two people involved in obtaining the diary pleaded guilty in August 2022; a court later allowed prosecutors to review the seized phones, but no charges were ever filed against O'Keefe himself, and he left Project Veritas in 2023 for unrelated reasons.
incidents.stated_justification: The search warrant cited a criminal investigation into the theft and interstate transport of Ashley Biden's diary; prosecutors did not separately justify seizing O'Keefe's phones rather than pursuing other investigative steps.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: A journalist's personal phones, containing what he said were confidential sources and reporting materials unrelated to the underlying investigation, were seized and later reviewed by federal prosecutors despite no charges ever being filed against him.

incidents.title: Hungary criminalizes false coronavirus information and grants Orban decree powers
incidents.summary: Hungary's parliament passed an emergency coronavirus law allowing prison terms of up to five years for spreading information the government deemed false or distorted about the pandemic, and let Prime Minister Viktor Orban rule by decree for an unlimited period.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The law was passed as Hungary, like much of Europe, entered its first coronavirus lockdown in March 2020; the government said it needed emergency powers to respond quickly to the pandemic.
incidents.what_happened: On March 30, 2020, Hungary's parliament passed a coronavirus emergency law criminalizing the publication of information the government deemed false or distorted about the pandemic, with penalties of up to five years in prison, and gave Prime Minister Viktor Orban the power to rule by decree for as long as the state of danger lasted, without a fixed end date. Reporters Without Borders said the law could let the government arbitrarily decide which reports were false and use that power against independent newsrooms. The International Press Institute said the law criminalized spreading information deemed to undermine the authorities' pandemic response, with fines and up to five years in prison. Under European pressure, Hungary's government said in late May 2020 it would ask parliament to end the decree powers by June 20, 2020, while the underlying criminal provision on false pandemic information remained on the books in a narrower form.
incidents.stated_justification: The government said the emergency powers and the criminal penalty for false pandemic information were necessary to respond quickly and combat what it called disinformation about the coronavirus.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Hungarian outlets faced the prospect of prison sentences for coronavirus reporting the government might later deem false or distorted, at the same time the government could rule by decree without a parliamentary check.
incidents.status: Hungary's government said in May 2020 it would ask parliament to end the decree powers by June 20, 2020; the sources reviewed did not establish the criminal provision's later fate in detail.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: Whether the criminal penalty for false pandemic information was narrowed or repealed after the state of danger ended was not established in the sources reviewed.

incidents.title: Myanmar junta revokes five outlets' licenses and raids newsrooms after coup
incidents.summary: Weeks after seizing power, Myanmar's military junta revoked the operating licenses of five independent media outlets covering protests against the coup and raided two of their newsrooms, seizing computers and files; journalists from the outlets were later arrested and charged under a broadened penal-code provision on spreading 'false news.'
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The outlets had been covering nationwide protests against the military's February 1, 2021 seizure of power from Myanmar's elected government, coverage the junta sought to stop by removing the outlets' legal authorization to operate.
incidents.what_happened: On March 8 and 9, 2021, Myanmar's military junta revoked the licenses of five independent outlets, Mizzima, Myanmar Now, 7Day News, Democratic Voice of Burma and Khit Thit Media, which had been covering protests against the February 1 coup. Soldiers and police raided Myanmar Now's Yangon office, seizing computers, documents and server equipment, and raided Mizzima's head office the following day. Two weeks after the coup, the junta had broadened Article 505(a) of the penal code to criminalize spreading what it called false news, raising the maximum penalty from two to three years in prison; journalists from the affected outlets were later arrested and charged under the provision while covering the protests. The Committee to Protect Journalists said the junta must immediately reverse the license suspensions and let the outlets resume normal operations.
incidents.stated_justification: Myanmar's Ministry of Information did not respond to CPJ's request for comment explaining the license revocations; the junta separately said in public statements that it respected media freedom while warning outlets against using words like "coup" and "junta."

incidents.title: Belarus blocks Tut.by and arrests its editors as 'extremist'
incidents.summary: Belarusian authorities blocked access to Tut.by, the country's most-read independent news site, searched its offices in three cities and arrested at least eleven staff, including its editor-in-chief, citing alleged media-law violations after the site had already lost its official media status.

incidents.title: Russia criminalizes 'fake' reporting on the military, up to 15 years in prison
incidents.summary: Russia's parliament passed a law criminalizing the publication of information about the military that contradicts official statements, with penalties up to 15 years in prison, prompting Novaya Gazeta to pull its Ukraine war coverage and the BBC, CNN and other outlets to suspend operations inside Russia.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The law followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, and was aimed at reporting on the war that differed from the Russian defense ministry's official statements about casualties and military conduct.

Parliament speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said the law was meant to protect Russian soldiers and the truth. Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia's few remaining independent outlets, removed its Ukraine war coverage from its site, warning that restrictions on reporting had moved from threats of blocking outlets to threats of criminal prosecution of journalists and ordinary citizens. The BBC suspended its Russian news operations, with director-general Tim Davie saying the safety of staff came first, and other foreign broadcasters and independent Russian outlets closed or left the country in the days that followed.

incidents.title: Indian tax authorities search BBC offices weeks after Modi documentary ban
incidents.summary: India's Income Tax Department searched BBC offices in Delhi and Mumbai for alleged tax evasion, three weeks after the government used emergency powers to block a BBC documentary examining Prime Minister Narendra Modi's response to 2002 communal violence.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The searches followed the government's ban, weeks earlier, of the BBC documentary 'India: The Modi Question,' which examined Modi's record as Gujarat's chief minister during 2002 riots that killed mostly Muslims.
incidents.what_happened: On February 14, 2023, India's Income Tax Department conducted what officials called surveys, sealing off and searching BBC offices in Delhi and Mumbai and confiscating documents and journalists' phones, in what the government said was an investigation into tax evasion. incidents.title: Bombay High Court strikes down India's government 'fact check unit' rule
incidents.summary: India's 2023 amendment to its Information Technology Rules empowered a government-run Fact Check Unit to label online content about the central government 'fake' or 'false' and require its removal; comedian Kunal Kamra and media groups challenged it, and the Bombay High Court struck the rule down as unconstitutionally vague.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The government said the Fact Check Unit was needed to combat misinformation about its own policies and announcements online, at a time when it separately faced criticism over content restrictions ahead of India's 2024 general election.
incidents.what_happened: In 2023, India's government amended its Information Technology Rules to create a Fact Check Unit empowered to identify online content about the central government's own affairs as "fake, false or misleading" and require platforms to remove it or lose their legal protection from liability for user content. Comedian Kunal Kamra, the Editors Guild of India and the Association of Indian Magazines challenged the rule, arguing there was no constitutional "right to the truth" that could justify a government body policing facts about itself. India's Supreme Court stayed the unit's operation while the case proceeded. After a split verdict, a tie-breaking judge on the Bombay High Court struck down the rule in September 2024, finding its key terms "vague and overbroad" and the government's own definition of misinformation legally unsound.
incidents.stated_justification: The government said the Fact Check Unit was needed to address "misinformation concerning the Central Government's affairs" and to identify content that was "fake" or "false."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Had it taken effect, the rule would have let a government body decide which online statements about its own policies counted as false and require platforms to remove them, a power that never came into force because of the legal challenge.
incidents.status: The rule was struck down; the Fact Check Unit never operated after the Supreme Court's stay.

incidents.title: Guatemala convicts investigative journalist Jose Ruben Zamora on money-laundering charge
incidents.summary: A Guatemalan court convicted El Periodico founder Jose Ruben Zamora of money laundering and sentenced him to six years in prison, months after his newspaper, known for investigating government corruption, was forced to close; press-freedom groups said the case was connected to his investigative reporting rather than the financial charge alone.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: El Periodico had published more than 120 investigations into government corruption since January 2020 before its forced closure in May 2023, shortly before Zamora's conviction.

Zamora had been arrested the previous July, and El Periodico, which had published more than 120 investigations into government corruption since January 2020, was forced to close in May 2023, with its leadership citing pressure on its advertisers and on its operations. Zamora said prosecutors had "treated us like criminals" and destroyed evidence; his son said the state had effectively kidnapped an innocent man. incidents.effect_on_reporting: One of Guatemala's most prominent investigative outlets closed and its founder was imprisoned within the same year, a sequence press-freedom groups said sent a message to other Guatemalan journalists covering official corruption.

incidents.title: Nicaragua strips 94 political opponents, including journalists, of citizenship

incidents.title: Georgia enacts 'foreign influence' law requiring media to register as foreign-backed

incidents.issue_of_the_day: The governing Georgian Dream party framed the law as protecting Georgian sovereignty against foreign-funded groups it accused of trying to organize unrest, at a time when the party also faced growing opposition ahead of Georgia's 2024 parliamentary election.

incidents.title: Hong Kong court convicts Stand News editors of sedition
incidents.summary: A Hong Kong court convicted former Stand News editors Chung Pui-kuen and Patrick Lam of conspiring to publish seditious material, under a colonial-era law, over articles the outlet had run before police raided its newsroom and it closed at the end of 2021.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The prosecution centered on opinion pieces and interviews Stand News had published examining Hong Kong's 2019 protests and the 2020 National Security Law, coverage prosecutors said smeared the security law and law enforcement.
incidents.what_happened: On August 29, 2024, Hong Kong District Court Judge Kwok Wai-kin convicted former Stand News editor-in-chief Chung Pui-kuen and acting editor-in-chief Patrick Lam of conspiring to publish and reproduce seditious material, finding that 11 of 17 articles the prosecution presented had been seditious under a sedition law dating to the colonial era. Stand News had already ceased operating in December 2021 after a police raid on its offices. Chung argued in response that free speech should not be limited to eliminating dangerous ideas but should instead be used to counter them. A U.S. State Department spokesperson said the verdict directly harmed media freedom. Both editors were sentenced on September 26, 2024, facing up to two years in prison.
incidents.stated_justification: The court found that the articles were seditious because they were capable of undermining public confidence in the Hong Kong or Chinese central government, and prosecutors argued certain pieces promoted ideologies the law prohibited or smeared the security law and police.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: A once-prominent Hong Kong outlet had already closed under police pressure, and the criminal conviction of its editors for material it had published established that ordinary opinion journalism about the security law could carry a prison sentence.
incidents.status: Both editors were sentenced in September 2024; the convictions were not overturned in the sources reviewed.
incidents.outcome_note: Both editors were sentenced in September 2024; no reversal of the convictions was reported.

incidents.title: Milei's government shuts down Argentina's state news agency Telam
incidents.summary: President Javier Milei's government fenced off and shut down Telam, Argentina's state-owned news agency, calling it a public-relations operation for the prior Kirchnerist governments; unions and journalist groups called the closure one of the most serious blows to press freedom in decades of Argentine democracy.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Milei had campaigned against what he called wasteful and politically one-sided state spending, and Telam, founded in 1945, had long been associated with the governments of the Kirchner political movement he defeated in the 2023 election.
incidents.what_happened: On the night of March 3 into March 4, 2024, Milei's government fenced off Telam's Buenos Aires offices and blocked staff from entering, taking the agency's website offline and placing its roughly seven hundred employees on seven days of paid leave while the closure proceeded. Milei said it was wrong for a poor country's government to spend public money buying journalists' favor, calling Telam "a covert propaganda ministry" and "a Kirchnerist propaganda agency for the last decades." The Buenos Aires Press Union, SiPreBA, called the closure one of the worst actions against freedom of expression in forty years of Argentine democracy, and the Argentine Journalism Forum, Fopea, said the decision would deepen intolerance toward journalism. Workers and press-freedom advocates organized protests, including a symbolic gathering around the building, but the closure proceeded.
incidents.stated_justification: Milei said it was "immoral that in a poor country like ours, the government spends the people's money to buy the will of journalists," describing Telam as "a covert propaganda ministry."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Argentina's national wire service, which many regional and local outlets relied on for national and international news feeds, stopped operating, and roughly seven hundred journalists and staff lost their positions.
incidents.status: Telam's newsroom remained closed; the agency was later reorganized as a smaller state communications operation.
incidents.outcome_note: Telam's original newsroom remained closed; the agency was later reorganized as a smaller state communications operation.

incidents.title: Serbian police strike, detain and disarm journalists covering anti-government protests
incidents.summary: The Committee to Protect Journalists documented at least 28 Serbian journalists reporting being struck, detained, sprayed with chemical irritants or having their equipment destroyed by police between June and September 2025 while covering nationwide anti-government protests; the interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The protests, which grew through the summer of 2025, followed months of demonstrations against President Aleksandar Vucic's government that began after a deadly railway-station canopy collapse in Novi Sad in late 2024.
incidents.what_happened: Between June and September 2025, Serbian police repeatedly used force against journalists covering nationwide anti-government protests, according to a Committee to Protect Journalists report published September 25, 2025 documenting at least 28 affected journalists. On September 5 in Novi Sad, police kicked reporter Emir Kahrimanovic despite his visible press vest, forced Vreme reporter Katarina Stevanovic to lie on the ground for about fifteen minutes, and grabbed and smashed KTV reporter Nemanja Sarovic's microphone while he was reporting live. On September 1, an officer seized Beta news agency reporter Bozidar Milovac's phone and forced him to delete footage despite his identifying himself as a journalist. In earlier incidents in Belgrade and other cities in July and August, reporters described being struck with batons and shields, sprayed with an unknown chemical substance, and having memory cards destroyed. CPJ's Europe representative called for swift, transparent investigations and accountability for the officers involved; the interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment.
incidents.stated_justification: No Serbian official offered a public justification for the specific incidents documented; the interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Journalists covering the protests described routinely facing physical force, confiscation or destruction of equipment, and orders to stop filming, even when visibly identified as press, narrowing on-the-ground coverage of the demonstrations.
incidents.status: No officer was reported disciplined for any of the documented incidents as of CPJ's report.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: Whether any internal investigation into individual officers' conduct was opened was not established in the source reviewed.
incidents.outcome_note: The interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment, and no officer was reported disciplined for the incidents documented.

incidents.title: Ethiopia arrests at least six journalists including Sheger FM staff over election-year coverage
incidents.summary: Ethiopian authorities arrested at least six journalists between August and September 2025, including three from Sheger FM after the Ethiopian Media Authority ordered the station to delete a broadcast it accused of bias and inciting violence, ahead of national elections scheduled for 2026.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The arrests came ahead of Ethiopia's national elections scheduled for 2026, after the Ethiopian Media Authority ordered Sheger FM to remove an August 29, 2025 broadcast it said was one-sided and incited violence.
incidents.what_happened: Between August and September 2025, Ethiopian authorities arrested at least six journalists and media workers, including radio host Khadar Mohamed Ismail on August 5, radio host Abdulsemed Mohammed on August 11, and journalist Yonas Amare, who was abducted on August 13 and released on August 22 along with Mohammed. On September 3, Sheger FM journalists Tigist Zerihun, Mintamir Tsegaw and Eshete Assefa were arrested after the Ethiopian Media Authority ordered the station to delete an August 29 broadcast it accused of bias and inciting violence. Human Rights Watch said the authorities' renewed efforts to limit independent reporting were aimed at preventing public scrutiny of the government ahead of elections scheduled for 2026, adding that a free press mattered more, not less, in the run-up to a vote. Some of the Sheger FM journalists were granted bail in mid-September while an appeal proceeded.
incidents.stated_justification: The Ethiopian Media Authority accused the Sheger FM broadcast of "bias and inciting violence" when it ordered the station to remove it.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Independent Ethiopian broadcasters described feeling pressure to delete their own content and hold back coverage under threat of arrest, narrowing reporting on politically sensitive events ahead of the 2026 election.
incidents.status: Some journalists were granted bail while an appeal proceeded; the media authority's order against Sheger FM remained in force.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The final legal outcome for each of the six journalists named was not established in the source reviewed.
incidents.outcome_note: Some journalists were granted bail while an appeal proceeded; the media authority's order against Sheger FM remained in force.

incidents.title: Pakistan amends cybercrime law to create new agency policing 'fake' online content
incidents.summary: Pakistan's parliament amended the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act to create a new Social Media Protection and Regulatory Authority with power to block online content and a Social Media Protection Tribunal, and made spreading information deemed 'fake or false' punishable by up to three years in prison, prompting nationwide journalist protests.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The government said the amendment was needed to curb online disinformation, but journalists said the new offense's vague wording, covering content merely believed likely to cause "fear, panic, disorder or unrest," gave authorities broad discretion over ordinary reporting.
incidents.what_happened: On January 29, 2025, Pakistan's parliament passed amendments to the 2016 Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act creating a government-appointed Social Media Protection and Regulatory Authority, empowered to order the removal or blocking of online content, and a separate Social Media Protection Tribunal to hear related cases. A new provision, Section 26A, made it a crime punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine of about $7,000 to knowingly disseminate information believed to be false or fake and likely to cause "fear, panic, disorder or unrest." The Pakistan Press Foundation said the lack of clarity around the amendments raised questions about the government's real intent, and Human Rights Watch called for the law's repeal, saying it lacked any exemption protecting journalistic work. The Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists organized nationwide protests, calling the law an infringement on people's rights.
incidents.stated_justification: The law's Section 26A targets the "intentional dissemination, exhibition or transmission of information...that the sender knows or believes to be false or fake and likely to cause or create a sense of public fear, panic, disorder or unrest."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Journalists faced a vaguely worded criminal offense, enforced by a government-appointed authority and tribunal rather than the courts, for publishing information officials could later deem false, with no exemption for journalistic work.
incidents.status: The amendment remained law despite the nationwide protests and Human Rights Watch's call for repeal.
incidents.outcome_note: The amendment remained law despite nationwide journalist protests and a Human Rights Watch call for its repeal.

incidents.title: Journalists beaten in Bangladesh in separate incidents as interim government drafts new cyber laws
incidents.summary: On a single day in February 2025, groups of men beat at least eight journalists in two separate incidents in rural Bangladesh while they investigated a medical-negligence tip and a land dispute; the incidents came as the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus drafted new cyber ordinances rights groups said could add legal risk on top of the physical one.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The incidents occurred six months into the interim government that took power after Sheikh Hasina's government fell in August 2024, a period in which press-freedom groups said journalists faced both continued street violence and new draft cyber-security legislation.
incidents.what_happened: On February 3, 2025, ten to twelve men beat Samakal correspondent Shohag Khan Sujon with a hammer and knife while he investigated allegations of medical negligence in Shariatpur district, and four other journalists who intervened were also beaten. The same day, in Laxmipur district, four correspondents covering a land dispute were beaten with bamboo sticks by a separate group that also fired guns, wounding one journalist with shrapnel. Days earlier, British freelance journalist Shafiur Rahman received threatening emails after publishing an article about a government security meeting, warning him to "stop or suffer the consequences." The Committee to Protect Journalists said the interim government's draft Cyber Protection Ordinance and Personal Data Protection Ordinance, introduced in January 2025, risked giving authorities broad new power over online content and user data on top of the continuing physical violence journalists faced covering local disputes.
incidents.stated_justification: No government official offered a public justification for the beatings, which were carried out by private individuals; the interim government described its draft cyber ordinances as necessary data-protection and security measures.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Reporters covering local corruption and land disputes in rural Bangladesh faced serious physical violence in a single day, while a freelance journalist covering national-security matters received written threats, illustrating the range of pressure facing the press during the political transition.
incidents.status: No arrests in the beatings were reported in the source reviewed, and the proposed cyber ordinances remained under review.
incidents.outcome_note: No arrests were reported in the incidents described, and the proposed cyber ordinances remained under review.

incidents.title: Venezuela detains, expels and restricts journalists after disputed 2024 election
incidents.summary: In the two weeks after Venezuela's disputed July 28, 2024 presidential election, Reporters Without Borders documented 70 press-freedom violations, including nine detentions, nine expulsions of foreign correspondents and the suspension of the social media platform X, as President Nicolas Maduro's government moved to control coverage of the disputed result.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Venezuela's July 28, 2024 election, in which the National Electoral Council declared Maduro the winner without releasing detailed vote tallies opposition figures disputed, triggered protests and a surge of restrictions on the journalists covering them.
incidents.what_happened: In the fifteen days after Venezuela's July 28, 2024 election, Reporters Without Borders documented 70 press-freedom violations, including 18 access restrictions, 30 cases of threats or coercion, nine detentions, nine expulsions of foreign journalists and four instances of physical violence. Colombian journalists Carolina Trinidad and Vanessa de la Torre were expelled from the Caracas airport without explanation on election day, Chilean journalists Ivan Nunez and Jose Luis Tapia were held incommunicado at a military post until their embassy intervened, and Spanish journalist Alvaro Nieto was deported after a two-hour interrogation. Venezuelan photojournalists and broadcasters, including Yousnel Alvarado and Deisy Pena, were detained and, in some cases, held on terrorism-related charges. The government also opened a criminal investigation into the opposition-aligned results website ResultadosConVzla, suspended X for ten days and blocked Signal and Reddit. RSF's Latin America director said the pattern of violations showed the government's determination to limit public debate.
incidents.stated_justification: No specific public justification for the individual detentions and expulsions was documented; the government separately described the platform suspensions as necessary to prevent the spread of what it called disinformation about the election.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Foreign correspondents were expelled or detained within days of the vote, Venezuelan journalists were jailed on serious charges including terrorism, and major communication platforms were blocked or suspended, sharply narrowing independent coverage of the disputed result.
incidents.status: Detained journalists faced continuing prosecution, and social-platform restrictions remained in place after the fifteen-day period RSF documented.
incidents.outcome_note: Detained journalists faced continuing prosecution, and social-platform restrictions remained in place after the documented period.

incidents.title: Turkish authorities detain three journalists under 'disinformation' law
incidents.summary: Turkish authorities detained three journalists, jailing columnist Tolga Sardan pending trial, under a 2022 law criminalizing the spread of disinformation, after the government's own disinformation-fighting body disputed their reporting on a leaked intelligence document and a story about released prisoners.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Sardan had written about an alleged Turkish intelligence report on judicial corruption, which the government's Center for Combating Disinformation denied existed; Halk TV's Dincer Gokce had reported on people released from prison who were later linked to further crimes.
incidents.what_happened: On November 1 and 2, 2023, Turkish authorities detained T24 columnist Tolga Sardan, Halk TV news editor Dincer Gokce and Kisa Dalga reporter Cengiz Erdinc under Turkiye's 2022 law criminalizing the spread of what officials call disinformation. Sardan was jailed pending trial after writing about an intelligence report on judicial corruption that the government's Center for Combating Disinformation said did not exist. Gokce was released after a court ordered him to read books about journalism, over an article about people released from prison who authorities said had been wrongly described. Erdinc was released the following day. The Committee to Protect Journalists called on Turkish authorities to release Sardan and Erdinc without delay and said the vague law would continue to stifle reporting in the country.
incidents.stated_justification: Turkey's Center for Combating Disinformation denied the existence of the intelligence report Sardan had written about, and authorities said Gokce's article about released prisoners had proven inaccurate.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: A columnist was jailed pending trial and another journalist was ordered by a court to read books about journalism, over stories the government's own disinformation body disputed rather than a court finding of falsity through an ordinary defamation process.
incidents.status: Two of the three detained journalists were released within a day or two; Sardan remained jailed pending trial.
incidents.outcome_note: Two of the three journalists were released within a day; Tolga Sardan remained jailed pending trial.

incidents.title: Tunisia's cybercrime decree pushes jailed-journalist count to highest since 1992
incidents.summary: The Committee to Protect Journalists found at least four journalists imprisoned under Tunisia's 2022 Decree-Law 54 on cybercrime as of January 2025, including radio hosts Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies, pushing the country's jailed-journalist count to its highest since 1992 under President Kais Saied.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Decree-Law 54, issued by President Kais Saied in 2022 without a sitting parliament, criminalized spreading what authorities deem "false news" online, and by January 2025 had become the basis for jailing a record number of Tunisian journalists.
incidents.what_happened: The Committee to Protect Journalists reported on January 16, 2025 that at least four of five imprisoned Tunisian journalists were convicted under Decree-Law 54, a 2022 cybercrime decree President Kais Saied issued while ruling by decree without a sitting parliament. Radio hosts Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies of IFM each received one-year sentences, commentator Sonia Dahmani's one-year sentence was reduced to eight months on appeal before she received an additional two-year sentence, and journalist Mohamed Boughaleb received six months on a separate defamation charge. The head of Tunisia's journalists' union, Ziad Debbar, said the decree had turned every journalist into a suspect. The International Commission of Jurists said Tunisian authorities were using the decree to arbitrarily restrict dissenting voices, in violation of the country's human rights obligations, subjecting journalists, politicians and rights defenders to prosecution, investigation and imprisonment.
incidents.stated_justification: Decree-Law 54 targets content that "produces, spreads, disseminates, sends or writes false news" seen as threatening "rights of others, public safety or national defense or sowing terror."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Tunisia, once cited as a rare post-Arab Spring press-freedom success, reached its highest count of imprisoned journalists since 1992, with radio hosts and commentators serving sentences of six months to more than two years for broadcast commentary and online statements.
incidents.status: Decree-Law 54 remained in force and continued to produce new prosecutions as of CPJ's report.
incidents.outcome_note: Decree-Law 54 remained in force and continued to produce new prosecutions, which CPJ said brought jailed-journalist numbers to a record.

incidents.title: Tanzania shuts down internet access on election day amid unrest
incidents.summary: Tanzania's government restricted internet and social-media access on October 29, 2025, as citizens voted in a general election marked by protests, cutting national internet traffic by nearly 90 percent and leaving both local and foreign journalists unable to report on the vote and its aftermath in real time.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The shutdown coincided with a disputed general election and protests against President Samia Suluhu Hassan's government, which Human Rights Watch later said was followed by killings and broader restrictions once the results were announced.
incidents.what_happened: On October 29, 2025, as Tanzanians voted in a general election, national internet traffic began falling sharply around 12:30 p.m. local time, dropping to nearly 90 percent below the previous week's levels, according to monitoring cited by TechCabal; three journalists in Dar es Salaam and Arusha said social media platforms were unreachable without a virtual private network. Neither the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority nor telecom operators responded publicly to questions about the outage, and Tanzanian authorities did not issue a statement explaining it. Human Rights Watch reported on November 4, 2025 that the shutdown prevented media from reporting on the election and the protests that followed, and said authorities appeared to have also blocked foreign journalists from covering the vote by not responding to their accreditation applications.
incidents.stated_justification: Tanzanian authorities did not issue a public statement explaining the internet restrictions.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Local and international journalists lost the ability to report in real time on the election and the protests that followed, while some foreign correspondents said their accreditation requests to cover the vote went unanswered.
incidents.status: Disruptions to social platforms continued for at least several days after the vote; authorities did not explain or formally end the restrictions.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The precise date full connectivity was restored was not established in the sources reviewed.
incidents.outcome_note: Authorities did not explain the shutdown, and disruptions to social platforms continued for several days after the vote.

incidents.title: Court orders RCMP to stop restricting press access at Fairy Creek logging blockades
incidents.summary: A British Columbia court found the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had failed to justify wide exclusion zones that kept journalists away from its enforcement of a logging injunction at the Fairy Creek old-growth blockades, and ordered police to keep the media's role in a free society in mind when deciding whether to remove or arrest reporters.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The RCMP was enforcing a court injunction won by logging company Teal-Jones against protesters blocking old-growth logging roads near Fairy Creek on Vancouver Island, and had required journalists to check in and stay escorted rather than observe enforcement directly.
incidents.what_happened: Through the summer of 2021, journalists covering the RCMP's enforcement of a court injunction against old-growth logging protesters at Fairy Creek, on Vancouver Island in British Columbia, said police required them to check in at set times and remain escorted rather than observe arrests directly, restricting their ability to independently document the operation. A coalition of Canadian news organizations went to court, and on July 20, 2021, Justice Douglas Thompson found the RCMP had not justified the extensive exclusion zones it had imposed on media access. The judge ordered that future enforcement decisions be made with an explicit reminder of the media's role in a free and democratic society and the need to avoid unnecessary interference with journalism. The RCMP had defended the restrictions as reasonably necessary given hazardous terrain, limited space for enforcement and poor cell coverage.
incidents.stated_justification: The RCMP said the restrictions were "reasonably necessary" because of hazardous terrain, limited space to safely conduct enforcement, and poor cell phone coverage at the blockade sites.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Journalists had been kept at a distance from arrests and enforcement actions for weeks under an escort system that limited independent verification of how the operation was being conducted, before the court intervened.
incidents.status: The court granted the media coalition's request; the RCMP was required to factor press access into future enforcement decisions.
incidents.outcome_note: The court granted the media coalition's request, requiring the RCMP to account for press access in future enforcement decisions.

incidents.title: Australia's High Court invalidates warrant for raid on journalist Annika Smethurst
incidents.summary: Australia's High Court ruled that the warrant the Australian Federal Police used to raid News Corp journalist Annika Smethurst's home over a national-security leak was invalid, and weeks later the AFP said it would not lay charges against her, citing insufficient evidence.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The 2019 raid stemmed from Smethurst's reporting on leaked, classified plans to expand the Australian Signals Directorate's domestic surveillance powers, which the government treated as a national-security leak investigation.
incidents.what_happened: The Australian Federal Police had searched journalist Annika Smethurst's Canberra home in 2019 over her reporting on leaked documents describing plans to expand the Australian Signals Directorate's powers to monitor Australians domestically. Smethurst challenged the warrant, and on April 15, 2020, Australia's High Court unanimously ruled it invalid because it failed to properly specify the offense being investigated, though the court allowed police to keep the seized material for any future prosecution. On May 27, 2020, AFP Deputy Commissioner Ian McCartney announced the agency would not charge Smethurst, saying there was insufficient evidence to establish the path the leaked document had taken or who had provided it. The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance said the case showed how national-security laws could be misused against legitimate public-interest journalism, and the Law Council of Australia's president said the law still left journalists exposed to investigation and prosecution.
incidents.stated_justification: The AFP said its investigation could not establish, with sufficient evidence, how the leaked document had moved or who had provided it to Smethurst.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: A journalist's home was searched and her devices seized over a story about government surveillance powers, and although the warrant was ultimately found invalid and no charges followed, press-freedom groups said the case showed reporters remained exposed to similar national-security investigations.
incidents.status: The AFP closed its investigation without charges after the High Court found the original warrant invalid.
incidents.outcome_note: The High Court found the 2019 warrant invalid, and the AFP announced weeks later it would not charge Smethurst.

incidents.title: China expels American journalists from three major U.S. newspapers
incidents.summary: China ordered American correspondents for The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post to leave the country, in a reciprocal response to the Trump administration capping the number of Chinese state-media employees allowed in the United States, which itself followed China's earlier expulsion of three Journal reporters over an opinion headline.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The expulsions followed a rapid exchange of measures: a Wall Street Journal opinion piece China objected to, the U.S. capping Chinese state-media staff, and China's decision to expel American reporters from three outlets in response, all unfolding as the coronavirus pandemic was spreading globally.
incidents.what_happened: In February 2020, after The Wall Street Journal published an opinion column China's government objected to, Beijing revoked the press credentials of three Journal reporters based in China. On March 2, 2020, the Trump administration capped the number of Chinese state-media employees allowed to work in the United States at 100, down from about 160. On March 17, 2020, China's foreign ministry announced it would require American journalists working for The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post whose press cards were due to expire that year to leave the country, and said they would not be allowed to work as journalists in mainland China, Hong Kong or Macau. China's foreign ministry called the move "entirely necessary and reciprocal countermeasures" against what it described as American measures aimed exclusively at Chinese media organizations. U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo said he regretted China's decision to further limit free press operations worldwide.
incidents.stated_justification: China's foreign ministry described the expulsions as "entirely necessary and reciprocal countermeasures," saying "what the US has done is exclusively targeting Chinese media organizations, and hence driven by a Cold War mentality."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: American correspondents for three of the country's largest newspapers lost their accreditation to report from mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau at the outset of the global coronavirus pandemic, cutting into independent Western reporting from China during a major global story.
incidents.status: The expelled journalists' credentials were not restored in the source reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The precise number of journalists affected across the three outlets was not specified in the source reviewed.
incidents.outcome_note: The expelled journalists' press credentials were not restored; reciprocal media restrictions between the two countries continued for years afterward.

incidents.title: Zimbabwe's Patriotic Act criminalizes journalists' contact with foreign governments
incidents.summary: President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed the Patriotic Act, which criminalizes meeting foreign governments or officials with intent to harm Zimbabwe's sovereignty, with penalties up to death for advocating armed intervention and up to ten years for supporting sanctions, weeks before the country's 2023 general election.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The bill passed weeks before Zimbabwe's August 2023 general election, at a time when the government accused foreign-linked civil-society and media figures of working to undermine it ahead of the vote.
incidents.what_happened: Zimbabwe's parliament passed the Criminal Law Amendment (Patriotic Act) in June 2023, and President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed it into law on July 14, 2023. The law criminalizes meetings with foreign governments or their agents intended to subvert, overthrow or damage Zimbabwe's sovereignty, with penalties as severe as life imprisonment or death for advocating armed intervention, and up to ten years in prison or a fine for advocating sanctions or trade boycotts against the country. The Committee to Protect Journalists' Angela Quintal said journalists must be free to report and meet whomever they choose, including foreign diplomats, without risking imprisonment, and called on Mnangagwa to reject the bill. Information Minister Monica Mutsvangwa said the law did not criminalize journalists' ordinary work but only meetings intended to injure the country's sovereignty. Zimbabwean journalist Dumisani Muleya asked whether an interview eliciting an unfavorable answer could itself be treated as a crime under the law.
incidents.stated_justification: Information Minister Monica Mutsvangwa said the bill "did not criminalize journalists' work in Zimbabwe but barred meetings with foreign governments...that have 'the intention to injure the sovereignty.'"
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Zimbabwean journalists who interview foreign diplomats or officials, a routine part of covering international affairs, faced the risk that authorities could later characterize such contact as intended to damage the country's sovereignty, carrying penalties as severe as life imprisonment.
incidents.status: President Mnangagwa signed the bill into law in July 2023 despite CPJ's call for a veto; a journalists' court challenge did not block it.
incidents.outcome_note: President Mnangagwa signed the bill into law despite CPJ's call for a veto; a court challenge by journalists did not block it.
